title: Evaluating the drug use “gateway” theory using cross-national data: Consistency and associations of the order of initiation of drug use among participants in the WHO world mental health surveys

claims.statement: In US adults who had used drugs at least 12 times, in Australian twins and in surveys in 17 countries, starting to use drugs young is associated with more drug problems later (lifetime drug use disorders in the US survey and in the twins, dependence in the 17-country surveys); none of the designs read can show whether starting young itself causes them. In a 1992 US national household survey (NLAES; 42,862 adults interviewed once; about 92% of selected households and 97% of selected people took part), 6,447 people (15.6%, weighted) had used drugs from any of ten classes, other than as prescribed, at least 12 times; 18.6% of them had had lifetime DSM-IV drug dependence and 20.1% drug abuse without dependence. Lifetime dependence was reported by 33.6% of those who recalled first using drugs at 13 or younger, 26.8% at 14, 25.4% at 15, 17.7% at 16 and between 11.4% and 15.1% at 17 or older (13.6% at 21 or older); abuse without dependence fell from 28.9% (13 or younger) to 13.6% (20). After adjustment for age group, sex, race, family history of alcoholism, duration of drug use and current or former use, the odds of lifetime dependence were about 4% lower, and of abuse about 5% lower, for each later year of first use (coefficients −0.04 and −0.05, SE 0.01; the abstract gives the two the other way round). The age of first use was recalled in the same interview as the diagnoses; the drug first used and the drug of the disorder are not linked; family drug problems, conduct problems and other psychiatric disorders were not measured; current or former use, one of the adjustments, may itself follow from the disorder; and the only prospective study the authors cite, which followed 15-year-old boys for 13 years, found that age at first use did not predict drug-related problems at 30, a result they discount (men only, a single 3-year window, an aggregate measure). The authors call early onset a powerful predictor, but ask whether the delay itself or, more likely, a combination of other factors lowers the risk, and call for prospective studies (Grant & Dawson, 1998). In the young-adult cohort of the volunteer Australian Twin Register (born 1964–1971; telephone interviews in 1996–2000 at a median age of 30; both twins took part in 69% of pairs), in 311 same-sex pairs in which one twin recalled first using cannabis before 17 and the co-twin did not (136 identical and 175 fraternal pairs; 234 co-twins started later and 77 never used cannabis), the twin who started early more often reported any illicit drug abuse or dependence (47.6% against 32.8%; conditional odds ratio 2.24, 95% CI 1.52 to 3.30), cannabis abuse or dependence (45.7% against 31.8%; 2.13, 1.45 to 3.13), alcohol dependence (42.8% against 29.6%; 2.17, 1.46 to 3.24) and use of other drug classes (2.57 to 5.15). Adjustment for differences between co-twins in early tobacco and alcohol use, conduct disorder, depression and social anxiety lowered the odds ratios by up to about a fifth (any drug abuse or dependence 1.98, 1.26 to 3.10; alcohol dependence 1.85, 1.21 to 2.83). Because co-twins grow up in the same home, the association is not explained by what they share; but factors that differ between co-twins, such as friends, were measured only in part and recalled at about 30, identical and fraternal pairs were pooled with no separate estimates for identical pairs, and 311 of the 407 discordant pairs counted in the paper's concordance analysis were analysed, without explanation. The authors read the results as consistent with a causal role and say that strong causal conclusions cannot be drawn from them alone (Lynskey et al., 2003). In pooled analyses of 17 WHO World Mental Health surveys (2001–2005; ages recalled at one interview), a later age at first use went with lower odds of later dependence (odds ratios 0.2 to 0.7 across the dependence outcomes, the unit not stated), and using more drug classes with higher odds, while starting drugs in an unusual order was largely unrelated to dependence (Degenhardt, Dierker, et al., 2010). Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
claims.magnitude: Grant & Dawson (1998), people who had used drugs at least 12 times, weighted prevalence of lifetime DSM-IV drug dependence by recalled age at first drug use (SE): 13 or younger 33.6% (1.9); 14, 26.8% (2.4); 15, 25.4% (1.9); 16, 17.7% (1.3); 17, 15.1% (1.4); 18, 15.0% (1.5); 19, 13.4% (1.9); 20, 11.4% (1.8); 21 or older 13.6% (1.2); abuse without dependence 28.9% (1.9) at 13 or younger to 13.6% (2.0) at 20 (the 11.1% printed for 21 or older is lower than all four subgroup values and is not used); adjusted coefficient per later year of first use −0.04 (SE 0.01) for dependence and −0.05 (0.01) for abuse, odds ratios about 0.96 and 0.95 per year (editors' conversion on the study card); overall, lifetime dependence 18.6% (0.6) and abuse 20.1% (0.6). Lynskey et al. (2003), 311 pairs, twin who started cannabis before 17 vs co-twin, lifetime prevalence and conditional odds ratio (95% CI), unadjusted; adjusted: any drug abuse or dependence 47.6% vs 32.8%, 2.24 (1.52–3.30); 1.98 (1.26–3.10); cannabis abuse or dependence 45.7% vs 31.8%, 2.13 (1.45–3.13); 1.96 (1.25–3.09); alcohol dependence 42.8% vs 29.6%, 2.17 (1.46–3.24); 1.85 (1.21–2.83); use of sedatives 2.83, hallucinogens 5.15, cocaine or other stimulants 4.19, opioids 2.57 (unadjusted). Degenhardt, Dierker, et al. (2010), pooled models of dependence onset, later age at first use, odds ratios 0.2 to 0.7 (unit not stated).

claims.statement: Evidence is insufficient to say whether using cannabis makes people more likely to go on to other illegal drugs (the 'gateway' idea), or whether the usual order of first use, and the link between the two, come from a shared liability to use drugs and from which drugs people are offered first. In the studies read, cannabis use usually came before other illegal drugs, except where cannabis was rare, and went with a much higher chance of using them. In New York State public high schools in 1971–1973 (5,468 students linked over 5 to 6 months, 66% of the students surveyed in the fall; students who could not be linked had used more drugs), 26% of the 558 students whose drug use had reached cannabis went on to another illegal drug within 5 to 6 months, mostly pills (12 percentage points) or psychedelics (9), with heroin about 2, against 4% of 2,911 students who had used only legal drugs and 1% of 482 who had used none; 56% stayed at cannabis and 19% used only legal drugs in the interval. These percentages were not adjusted for anything; the abstract calls cannabis a crucial step towards other illegal drugs, while the text says a drug does not invariably lead to the next and that the stages are probably culturally determined (Kandel, 1975). In four US household surveys (1991–1994; 44,624 people aged 12 to 25; ages recalled in whole years; people compared within neighbourhood and survey year, with sex, race or ethnicity and age group adjusted for, but no measure of individual liability), people who had used cannabis were more likely to have had a first chance to try cocaine (relative risk 4.6, 95% CI 3.8 to 5.6, without alcohol or tobacco use; 7.6, 6.9 to 8.4, with it; against people who had used none of the three) and, once offered, about 15 times as likely to start (11.3 to 19.8), also when the 73% who started in the same year as their first offer were left out (20.4, 10.2 to 40.7); about half of the people who had used cannabis started cocaine within 2 years of a first offer, against under 10% of the others many years later (Wagner & Anthony, 2002). In Australian twins born 1964–1971 (311 same-sex pairs in which one twin, but not the other, recalled first using cannabis before 17; interviewed at about 30), the twin who started early more often reported later use of other drugs (for example cocaine or other stimulants 47.9% against 26.4%, conditional odds ratio 4.19, 95% CI 2.60 to 6.75; hallucinogens 5.15; sedatives 2.83; opioids 2.57); the odds ratios stayed between 2.3 and 5.2 after adjustment for measured differences between the twins, and between 2.3 and 3.9 (unadjusted) in the 234 pairs in which both twins had used cannabis. The link is therefore not explained by what co-twins share, such as their upbringing; but identical and fraternal pairs were pooled, with no separate estimates for identical pairs, and differences between co-twins such as their friends were not measured; the authors call the results consistent with a causal role, perhaps through the social setting of cannabis use and access to other drugs, and say that strong causal conclusions cannot be drawn from them alone (Lynskey et al., 2003). A simulation of US young people, calibrated to household surveys of 1982–1994, in which one shared liability brings forward both the chances to use and the use of all drugs and cannabis has no effect by design, produced a strong relative risk of using heroin, cocaine or hallucinogens after cannabis (157, against 24 in the surveys), an order in which those drugs rarely come first (11 per 1,000, against 16 in the surveys) and a rise with cannabis frequency, and adjusting for an imperfect measure of that liability left large associations; it shows that these patterns cannot by themselves identify a cause, but it was not compared with a model that includes one, and its authors think something like a gateway effect probably exists through contact with illegal markets (Morral et al., 2002). In 17 WHO surveys (2001–2005; ages recalled at one interview), the order depended on how common each drug was: other illegal drugs came before cannabis in 11.4% (USA) and 12.7% (New Zealand) of people who had used them by 29, against 83.2% in Japan and 77.8% in Nigeria, where cannabis was rare (13 of 16 and 7 of 8 people); the link of cannabis with later other drug use was weaker where cannabis was more common, while that of alcohol or tobacco with later other drug use was stronger where those were more common; and starting in an unusual order was largely unrelated to later dependence (Degenhardt, Dierker, et al., 2010). A narrative review by proponents of a shared liability argues that the order need not reflect causal steps and calls that liability empirically proven, but does not discuss the co-twin evidence (Vanyukov et al., 2012). No study read separated a causal effect, a shared liability and access to drugs in one design, and all their data were collected between 1971 and 2005. Certainty: very low. Status: contested.
claims.magnitude: Not estimable as a causal effect. Kandel (1975), 5–6 months, unadjusted: moved beyond cannabis 26% of 558 students at the cannabis step (pills 12, psychedelics 9, cocaine 2, heroin 2 percentage points) vs 4% of 2,911 who had used only legal drugs and 1% of 482 who had used none; started cannabis 27% (N≥342) after beer or wine, cigarettes and hard liquor vs 2% (N≥467) after no drug. Wagner & Anthony (2002), relative risks (95% CI): first chance to try cocaine, against people who had used none of alcohol, tobacco or cannabis, 1.9 (1.7–2.1) after alcohol or tobacco only, 4.6 (3.8–5.6) after cannabis only, 7.6 (6.9–8.4) after both; starting cocaine once offered, cannabis vs none, 15 (11.3–19.8), and 20.4 (10.2–40.7) without people who started in the same year as the offer (73% of people who used cocaine); about 50% of people who had used cannabis started within 2 years of a first offer vs under 10% of others many years later. Lynskey et al. (2003), 311 discordant pairs, twin who started cannabis before 17 vs co-twin, lifetime prevalence and conditional odds ratio, unadjusted (adjusted): sedatives 19.0% vs 8.4%, 2.83 (2.28); hallucinogens 35.4% vs 18.0%, 5.15 (5.15); cocaine or other stimulants 47.9% vs 26.4%, 4.19 (4.06); opioids 13.5% vs 6.4%, 2.57 (2.34); in 234 pairs in which both used cannabis, unadjusted 3.00, 3.92, 3.00 and 2.33. Morral et al. (2002), simulation with no gateway effect vs US surveys: relative risk of heroin, cocaine or hallucinogens by 21 after cannabis by 21, 157 vs 24; one of those drugs at least a year before cannabis, 11 vs 16 per 1,000; odds ratio 297 with no adjustment, 82 after adjustment for a liability measure of reliability 0.8; no uncertainty intervals. Degenhardt, Dierker, et al. (2010): other illegal drugs before cannabis among people who used them by 29, USA 11.4%, New Zealand 12.7%, Japan 83.2% (13 of 16 people), Nigeria 77.8% (7 of 8); cannabis and later other illegal drugs at 18–29, odds ratio 7.4 (1.8–30.4) in the Netherlands vs 107.1 (57.9–198.1) in the USA; pooled interaction of cannabis use with cannabis prevalence 0.3 (0.2–0.6), of alcohol or tobacco use with their prevalence 32.7 (8.3–129.0), scale not stated.
